item.title: CDVS Workshop: Story Maps — Thu Sep 17, 1:00 PM — Online
item.description:
This workshop will help you get started telling stories with maps on the ArcGIS StoryMaps platform. This easy-to-use web application combines interactive maps with narrative text, images, and videos to provide a powerful communication tool for any project with a spatial component. item.title: SHORT COURSE: Innovative Methods for Survey Weighting — Thu Sep 17, 1:00 PM — None
item.description:
*includes a 30 minute break* Learn more and register: https://ssri.duke.edu/talk-when-are-polling-differences-true-public-opinion-change/
This workshop will cover the foundations of survey weighting together with several modern, data-driven techniques.
We'll begin with survey sampling designs and design-based inference, including Horvitz-Thompson and Hájek estimators and the design weights that underlie them. We then examine survey nonresponse, coverage error, and nonprobability samples, along with standard approaches including inverse propensity weighting, post-stratification, linear weighting (GREG), and raking.
The workshop also covers practical considerations such as how weighting affects precision, what to weight on, when to trim, and how to assess balance. The workshop also focuses on advanced weighting techniques, including multilevel calibration weighting and kernel population weighting. item.title: Worlds of 1776 | Sarah Pearsall, “How the World Made the American Revolution” — Thu Sep 17, 1:30 PM — Smith Warehouse
item.description: Join us for conversation with Professor Sarah Pearsall (Johns Hopkins University) about her new book Freedom Round the Globe: A World History of the American Revolution In this powerful new history of the American Revolution, Sarah M. S. Pearsall argues that the American Founding Fathers did not have a unique claim on the revolutionary spirit. The thirteen colonies that became the United States, she reminds us, were not even half of the British colonies that existed in the eighteenth century. In her sparkling and original Freedom Round the Globe, Pearsall uncovers the insurgents, freedom lovers, and dreamers in India, West Africa, North America, Europe, China, and West Indian islands who shaped the nature of American rebellion and nationhood. Sarah M.S. Pearsall is Professor and Chair of History at Johns Hopkins University; she previously taught for nearly a decade at Cambridge University. The Graduate School is excited to invite the community to the 100 Years of Innovation: Duke Graduate Research Fair, occurring during Duke's Homecoming celebrations on Thursday, September 17 from 2-4 p.m.

item.title: Distinguished Seminar Series with Jeff Lichtman — Thu Sep 17, 3:00 PM — Wilkinson 021
item.description:
A central challenge in brain science is the relation between the structure and the function of the nervous system. Modern approaches to this problem get inspiration from the efforts of Cajal, more than 100 years, ago to map neural connections, but his work was insufficient in many ways. Now, with the advent of complete high-resolution descriptions of brain structure in which all the brain's synaptic wiring can in principle be mapped (connectomics), new technical and interpretive problems arise. Currently, whole brain connectomics is just getting underway and many bioengineering and computational challenges will need to be met before entire mammalian brains are mapped at the level of synapses. Perhaps the most significant of these challenges is how we extract understanding from the unprecedented complexity and size of the datasets coming our way.
Jeff W. Lichtman M.D., Ph.D. is Jeremy R Knowles Professor of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Ramon y Cajal Professor of Arts and Sci

item.title: Duke Arts Presents: shirlette ammons: Language Barrier at 10 — Thu Sep 17, 7:30 PM — Page Auditorium
item.description:
Ten years after the release of her acclaimed album Language Barrier, Durham-based poet, musician, and producer shirlette ammons brings the project home for a special full-album performance at Page Auditorium. In this one-night-only event, each track will be reimagined live with a rotating lineup of collaborators, reflecting the community spirit at the heart of the original recording. Guest artists include Lizz Wright, Mykki Blanco, Phil Cook, Cyanca, H.C. McEntire, Median, Sonny Miles, and Rissi Palmer.
Blending hip hop, rock, soul, and experimental sound, Language Barrier is a fearless crossing of musical and cultural lines and a poignant exploration of identity and belonging. A decade after its release, this hometown gathering revives the album into a living testament to the power of collaboration and connection - a timely reflection as the nation marks 250 years.
Source: Duke University

item.description:
Durham Writers Group We will be at the Moon House at 3039 University Dr. in Durham. This venue does not serve food or drink, but feel free to bring your own. There is a kitchenette for our use, but be sure to clean up afterwards. The space might be a little cozy; please consider masking or staying home if you have a respiratory ailment.
This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.
Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Tue Dec 15 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

item.title: Digital Accessibility Pop-Up Labs — Tue Dec 15, 11:00 AM — Carolina Union
item.description:
The POP Lab is a drop-in workspace where UNC faculty and staff can make progress with support from digital accessibility consultants. Bring your documents, course materials, websites, reports, or questions, and work at your own pace. Come by for a few minutes or stay for the full session to ask questions, explore tools, solve problems and make meaningful progress toward expanding access.
Progress Over Perfection
Progress means recognizing common barriers in the platforms you use and taking small steps to reduce them. It’s choosing web formats over PDFs, applying table headers, checking color contrast and collaborating on accessible templates so everyone can start from a strong foundation. Digital accessibility depends on steady, intentional progress, not perfection, to expand access for all.
Source: UNC Chapel Hill
